analysis: Only BASE text of .github/workflows/ci.yml and a truncated patch excerpt were supplied, so the head workflow was not fully visible. The visible patch shows these changes: a SAVE_CACHES env that is true only for pushes to refs/heads/master or refs/heads/dev; a CHECKOUT_SPARSE variable that excludes docs/reports/*.gz and landing videos; and the start of a new .git cache restore flow (actions/cache/restore pinned to a SHA, path .git, key git-v1-...). Per the patch comments, a failed restore discards the cache and checks out cold, and .git is saved daily per branch. The design appears to keep pull requests restore-only, so PR-controlled code should not poison caches that later privileged runs on master or dev restore. That depends on every save step being gated on SAVE_CACHES, and the rest of the head diff (about 1200 lines) was not visible. In the base text, the existing cluster-metadata cache save is already gated on push or on pull_request with no matched key, and the new SAVE_CACHES gating would tighten that. Newly added actions are SHA-pinned, and permissions stay contents: read. No provider runtime, coordinator contract, attestation, key custody or prefix-cache code is touched (T-041 was supplied but the diff does not alter it). I found no concrete regression against the threat model, which scopes CI only through the signed-artifact and release-qualification contract. Open integration questions for later passes: (1) whether every cache/save step and the release or signing workflows use SAVE_CACHES and cannot restore a .git or build cache written by an untrusted ref; (2) whether the sparse checkout excludes anything that the release-integrity, signing or qualification scripts read; (3) whether restoring an old .git can leave stale refs or objects that affect provenance checks such as check-release-version.sh. None of these is established as a vulnerability from the supplied evidence.
